11000.event: You hear the Netherlands is building floating neighbourhoods along its coast — half the world’s flood-prone cities want to copy them now.

11001.event: North America’s Great Famine hits in 2025. Rubbish becomes treasure overnight — everything’s a resource when nothing’s left. Even the air has a price tag now.

11002.event: The Cities of Climate Action hold their summit in a virtual room this year — no flights, no footprint. “Planet first,” they call it, above everything else.

11003.event: The UN creates a Parliament of the Commons — the oceans, the forests, the atmosphere all get their own flag and a seat at the table now.

11004.event: After the 35th Olympics, they scrap the whole committee. Too many athletes competing on bioengineered limbs — nobody could agree where fair play ends.

11005.event: The black market outgrows every legal market combined. You stop asking where things come from.

11006.event: New “resilience” building codes go up everywhere. Beijing, Shanghai, Tokyo, Delhi seal themselves under smog domes now — assuming you can afford to live inside one.

11007.event: Most of your protein comes from a lab now. Everyone’s saving the planet, and nobody’s noticed a whole generation coming down with the same deficiencies.

11008.event: One in five people you know live with a mental health disorder. Most of them are women. Most of them are medicated just to get through the day.

11009.event: Someone dies by suicide somewhere in the world every twenty seconds now. You try not to do the maths on how many that is by dinnertime.

11010.event: The big concrete manufacturers pledge 100% renewable energy. You’ll believe it when you see it.

11011.event: Cocaine, opioids, heroin — all legal now, across half the countries you’d ever want to live in.

11012.event: Nearly a quarter of a million people die of overdoses this year. Most of them younger than fifty.

11013.event: Divorce rates triple. There’s a new word now for people who remarry someone of the opposite sex to their last partner — everyone uses it like a punchline.

11014.event: Virgin plastic gets banned worldwide. Everything you own is made from something that already existed once.

11015.event: Oranges grow in Scandinavia now. Nobody where you live seems to find that as strange as you do.

11016.event: Female life expectancy climbs ten years — assuming you’ve got the bank account to match a healthy body.

11017.event: A new epidemic breaks out of Toronto’s Chinatown and doesn’t let go for two years.

11018.event: The second “People First, Not Planet” march fills the streets of every climate city. The world quietly agrees to let the temperature climb another degree anyway.

11019.event: Five billion of us wear mind-reading helmets now, just to change the channel without lifting a finger.

11020.event: You haven’t held a pen in three years. Neither has most of the world, apparently.

11021.event: Retirement age climbs to seventy almost everywhere. You do the maths on how many more years that is.

11022.event: School is a database now. A system decides exactly what you should know and by when — the only children who still get a real teacher are the rich ones.

11023.event: Everyone you know wears a sensor that already knows what disease might kill them, and roughly when.

11024.event: One in three newborns is genetically engineered now. The rich countries panic and pass laws — a little late to close a gap that wide.

11025.event: Dataism, born in China, becomes the world’s biggest religion. You’re not sure when exactly you started believing too.

11026.event: Digital doctors take over most diagnoses now — fewer mistakes, they say, and somehow kinder ones too.

11027.event: China and Taiwan tip the world into a second Cold War. Everyone not standing on either side quietly gets rich.

11028.event: Digital lawyers make the courts faster and fairer. Millions of very educated people join you in having nothing useful left to sell.

11029.event: Three billion people have a sleep implant now, timing their rest down to the minute. You still just lie awake.

11030.event: Twenty-five million people a year swap a body part for something that works better. Even hearts. Even brains.

11031.event: Algorithms replace democracy and the market both. Most people seem relieved to stop having to choose anything themselves.

11032.event: Two-thirds of the artists you know use an AI implant now, just to make “better” art. You still can’t tell whose work is whose anymore.

11033.event: The UN Security Council gets rebuilt from scratch — Japan, India, an African council, an Islamic council, a reunited Europe, the US, China, Russia.

11034.event: Humans aren’t allowed to drive anymore. Every car on the road is networked now — nobody you know has seen a crash in years.

11035.event: You realise you can’t survive anymore without staying connected to the network that already knows everything about everyone.

11036.event: They call it Cyber 911 — the day governments try to shut the global network down for twenty-four hours, just to prove they still can. They can’t.

11037.event: Liberalism quietly dies. The network already knows you better than you know yourself — there’s not much left to be liberated from.

11038.event: Most of us stop mattering, economically or militarily. A new class of upgraded elites owns all the data, commands the armies, and preaches Dataism from the top.

11039.event: The global birth rate drops to 1.2 children per woman. Nobody around you seems to be having any either.

11040.event: Night vision, a sharper sense of smell, better dreams — all products on a shelf now. Your memory’s going, so you buy the cloud drive everyone else has.

62006.event: You fall for your best friend — the girl, not the boy, though the three of us are close. You tell them both, separately. They’re kind about it. She turns you down gently; she already loves someone, she says. You think it might be him.

62007.event: You visit a lesbian bar for the first time in your life and make more friends than you expected. Introducing yourself as “boi” or “femme” still feels clumsy in your mouth, though. You’re working on it.

62008.event: Your friends talk about their futures — married, children, giving up work to keep house. None of it is the life you want. Your mum keeps asking if you have a boyfriend yet, and you keep changing the subject.

62009.event: You’re warned that coming out at work could get you fired on the spot — there’s no law here to stop them.

62010.event: Japan legalises same-sex marriage. There are protests out in the countryside, but in Tokyo the rainbow flags are already flying.

62011.event: You take a trip to Taiwan, just to see somewhere new for once.

62012.event: Japan’s population falls to 119.2 million. You read the headline twice.

62013.event: You have your first designer baby and go straight back to work.

62014.event: Japan’s population falls to 59.72 million now. Half of what it was.

71001.event: You start wearing a black veil now. Last spring, suicide attackers killed dozens of your classmates, but you still went back — you want to finish school, become a nurse. It’s the only way out you can see.

71002.event: You’re told this is your last year of school.

71003.event: You’re made to wear a burka now — the whole body, the whole head, just a strip of netting to see through. Your mother warns you never to take it off outside. The Taliban will shoot you if you don’t.

71004.event: You buy a book from the black market — a woman’s face on the cover, which is banned now, women aren’t allowed to be photographed or printed anymore. It’s written in English, and you don’t understand a word. You hide it and read it every night anyway.

71005.event: You’re married to a man your parents chose. Sex is something you dread — the first time most of all.

71006.event: Your husband decides you’re seeing other men. He whips you and calls you a “stupid, ugly whore,” then rapes you while you’re pregnant. You feel the shame of it for a long time after.

71007.event: Your first child arrives, and the world tilts a little on its axis.

71008.event: You lean over the balcony for a breath of fresh air. Someone reports you — women aren’t allowed to do that anymore — and you’re arrested.

71009.event: You try to run from your husband, from the violence. You’re caught. They lock you in a dark room, curtains drawn, for months.

71010.event: After praying, you set yourself on fire in front of your son — you can’t take your husband’s abuse any longer. You wake up in hospital, wrapped in bandages over third-degree burns. Your husband and father-in-law call to blame you. You wish it had worked.

71011.event: Feminist activists get your husband arrested. The local authorities let him go soon after. His family forbids you from seeing your son.

71012.event: His family finally lets you see your son again — on the condition that you sell yourself and beg on the street to support them, with your son beside you.

71013.event: Your sister is stoned to death. She was accused of sleeping with someone outside the marriage she never chose.

71014.event: You paint your nails anyway, knowing they’ll cut off your fingers if anyone sees. You’d rather lose the fingers than keep living as a slave in your husband’s house.

71015.event: You get your divorce. You know it means you’ll never see your son again.

72005.event: You realise you don’t want men — that you’re drawn to women instead. Your parents are already arranging your marriage to one.

72006.event: Your husband decides you’re seeing other men. He whips you and calls you a “stupid, ugly whore,” then rapes you while you’re pregnant. You feel the shame of it for a long time after.

72007.event: Your first child arrives, and the world tilts a little on its axis.

72008.event: You lean over the balcony for a breath of fresh air. Someone reports you — women aren’t allowed to do that anymore — and you’re arrested.

72009.event: You tell your closest friend the truth — that you feel for her the way a boy is supposed to feel for a girl. She pulls away at first. Later, she comes back, and we become something more. We manage to meet once or twice a week. No one can ever know.

72010.event: After praying, you set yourself on fire in front of your son — you can’t take your husband’s abuse any longer. You wake up in hospital, wrapped in bandages over third-degree burns. Your husband and father-in-law call to blame you. You wish it had worked.

72011.event: Feminist activists get your husband arrested. The local authorities let him go soon after. His family forbids you from seeing your son.

72012.event: His family finally lets you see your son again — on the condition that you sell yourself and beg on the street to support them, with your son beside you.

72013.event: A friend we both know, from our small hidden circle, is hanged — found out as a lesbian. Your partner and you decide it’s too dangerous now. We stop seeing each other.

72014.event: You paint your nails anyway, knowing they’ll cut off your fingers if anyone sees. You’d rather lose the fingers than keep living as a slave in your husband’s house.

72015.event: You get your divorce. You know it means you’ll never see your son again.

71016.event: University, gone. Your job at the NGO, gone. Then one morning you arrive to find every beauty salon in the country shut for good — sixty thousand of us lose our only wage in a single order.

72016.event: University, gone. Your job, gone. You grieve alone, quietly — the same new law that shut the salons spells out exactly what happens to women like you, if anyone ever finds out.

71017.event: Nursing was the last door left open to you — until they close that too. Years later, even the salary for staying home stops arriving. No warning. Nothing left to lose.

72017.event: Nursing was the last door left open to you — until they close that too. With no income and nowhere to hide, staying invisible gets harder every year. Invisible is the only way you’re safe.

21015.event: Roe falls. Within a year, your state bans abortion almost entirely. When you need one, you order pills online from a clinic three states over and pray your phone never gets subpoenaed.

22013.event: Roe falls the same year your state bans gender-affirming care outright. Two different laws, one message: your body isn’t yours to decide about. You start driving three states over for your prescriptions.

31012.event: A new law promises to punish workplace harassment. At your next interview they ask if you’re planning to marry and have kids soon. You hesitate — and the job quietly disappears.

32017.event: A new law promises to punish workplace harassment — it says nothing about you. The dating app you use vanishes from the App Store overnight, no explanation given. You already know why.

31013.event: You post online about not wanting children. By morning the post is gone, and so is your account, for a week. The platform calls it “provoking gender antagonism.”

32018.event: You post something small and rainbow-coloured for Pride. By morning it’s gone, and so is the account of the group that shared it. Nobody official ever explains why.

51010.event: A new law finally lets you pass your own nationality to your children — something only fathers could do before. At home, the century-old obedience clause hasn’t moved an inch.

52012.event: A new law lets mothers pass on their nationality at last. You barely notice — you deleted every dating app on your phone the year you heard about the men who didn’t.

41111.event: Parliament passes the Women’s Reservation Bill after twenty-seven years of trying — a third of all seats, promised to women like you. The fine print says it waits for a census nobody’s scheduled yet.

42107.event: The Supreme Court hears your case and agrees you face real discrimination — then rules, 3 to 2, that marriage still isn’t yours to have. That’s for Parliament to decide, they say. Parliament says nothing.

61015.event: You want to keep your own name when you marry. Japanese law still says one surname per couple — in practice, it’s always the wife’s that disappears. Parliament “continues discussions.”

62015.event: Your city hands you a partnership certificate, with real pride. It gets you nothing a marriage would — no inheritance, no next-of-kin rights. Court after court calls the ban unconstitutional. Nothing changes for you yet.

61016.event: You read that Japan has finally rewritten its century-old rape law — raising the age of consent, criminalising sex without consent for the first time. It took a wave of acquittals to shame them into it.

62016.event: Japan passes its first national law about people like you. It calls discrimination “unacceptable” and asks everyone to “endeavour” toward understanding — nothing about actually stopping it. You’re still waiting for the part with teeth.

21016.event: You work in the company’s diversity office — until a memo arrives one Monday morning ending the whole department, effective immediately. You clear out your own desk.

22014.event: The company’s LGBTQ+ staff network is one of the first things cut when the diversity office closes for good. The rainbow lanyard in your desk drawer suddenly feels like something you should hide.

22015.event: Your school tells your parents who you really are before you ever get the chance to yourself. The same week, the state votes to ban you from the girls’ changing room for good.

21017.event: Your uncle stops coming to Thanksgiving after the shouting match about the election. Your mum says it’s for the best. Nobody at the table agrees anymore on what “best” even means.

22016.event: Your uncle spends the whole of Thanksgiving arguing that people like you are what’s wrong with the country. Your mum finally tells him to leave. He doesn’t come back next year, and you find you don’t miss him.

21018.event: Your little brother buys a pill online, just to try it once. It’s cut with fentanyl. He doesn’t wake up the next morning.

22017.event: Your little brother buys a pill online, just to try it once. It’s cut with fentanyl. He doesn’t wake up the next morning.

11041.event: Overdose deaths finally start falling for the first time in years, down almost a quarter from the peak. It doesn’t feel like relief to the families who buried someone before the numbers turned.
